metadata.title: PIRLS 2001 User Guide for the International Database

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The PIRLS 2001 international database is built from a two-stage stratified cluster sample: schools are sampled first (with probability-proportional-to-size), and intact fourth-grade classes are sampled within schools. To support population-representative estimates, the user guide provides student sampling weights as composites of school, class, and student selection probabilities with non-response adjustments, including TOTWGT (total student weight), SENWGT (senate weight for equal country contribution), and HOUWGT (house weight for using sample size in variance estimation). For variance estimation under the complex design, the guide specifies jackknife repeated replication (JRR) using replicate-weight construction based on sampling zones (JKZONE) and replicate indicators (JKREP), with macros (e.g., JACKPV, JACKGEN) that generate replicate weights and compute sampling and imputation variance components. The guide does not present a single empirical analysis with a specific weight variable; instead, it documents which weights and replicate variables should be used depending on whether analyses are student-level, teacher-linked, or school-weighted, and whether plausible values are involved.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a user guide/technical documentation rather than an empirical predictive study. It describes plausible values generation for PIRLS achievement using multiple imputation (five plausible values) and the associated variance-combining logic, but it does not specify a single missing-data handling strategy for questionnaire item nonresponse in the way an empirical ML paper would (e.g., listwise vs multiple imputation for missing covariates). Therefore, missing_data_handling is not reported as a concrete analytic choice.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: This is a database user guide, not an empirical analysis paper. It documents that PIRLS 2001 assessed fourth-grade students (the upper of the two grades with the most 9-year-olds) using a two-stage sampling design (schools, then intact classes) and that within-school exclusions were limited to students with specified disabilities and non-native-language speakers who could not overcome the language barrier. It also explains that in secondary analyses, users should apply appropriate student filters (e.g., selecting the target grade via IDGRADER) and handle missing/omitted/not-administered codes according to the codebook conventions, and should use the provided sampling weights and JRR replicate variables when estimating standard errors.

data.outcome_summary: This PIRLS 2001 Database User Guide documents how the PIRLS 2001 reading literacy assessment was designed, administered, scaled, and how the international database should be analyzed. PIRLS 2001 assessed fourth-grade students using a matrix-sampling test design: each student completed two 40-minute reading blocks (one booklet per student) drawn from a larger pool of literary and informational passages, with both multiple-choice and constructed-response items. Achievement was scaled using item response theory (2PL/3PL for dichotomous items and a generalized partial credit model for polytomous constructed-response items) and proficiency estimates were produced via multiple imputation plausible values (five PVs) to support valid population inference under matrix sampling. The guide specifies international benchmarks (25th/50th/75th/90th percentiles) computed across plausible values and provides detailed instructions for complex survey variance estimation using jackknife repeated replication (JRR) with sampling zones (JKZONE) and replicate indicators (JKREP). It also explains how to use sampling weights (TOTWGT/SENWGT/HOUWGT) and how to interpret missing/omitted/not-administered codes in the database.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a technical user guide for the PIRLS 2001 international database rather than an empirical study that trains or evaluates predictive models. As a result, there is no analytic ML target variable, no reported model performance metrics, and no single analytic sample definition with per-country N for a specific secondary analysis. The guide instead provides the methodological machinery (sampling weights, JRR replicate weights, plausible values generation, and benchmark definitions) needed for downstream empirical analyses by other researchers.
